heading.en: Two ways to the same answer

hook.en: To check whether 97 is prime, you could divide it by every number from 2 to 96, or stop at 9. Both give the right answer. Which algorithm is better, and how do we know it is right?
hook.kn: 97 ಅವಿಭಾಜ್ಯವೇ ಎಂದು ತಿಳಿಯಲು 2 ರಿಂದ 96 ರವರೆಗಿನ ಎಲ್ಲಾ ಸಂಖ್ಯೆಗಳಿಂದ ಭಾಗಿಸಬಹುದು, ಅಥವಾ 9 ರಲ್ಲೇ ನಿಲ್ಲಿಸಬಹುದು. ಯಾವ ಕ್ರಮಾವಳಿ ಉತ್ತಮ, ಮತ್ತು ಅದು ಸರಿ ಎಂದು ಹೇಗೆ ತಿಳಿಯುವುದು?

body.en: An algorithm is verified before it is coded, to make sure it gives the correct output for all valid inputs. A common method is a dry run: we take sample inputs, execute each step by hand and record the values of the variables in a table. Inputs should include normal values and boundary cases such as 0, 1 or the largest value.

title.en: On the board: Dry run and comparing three prime tests

say.en: To verify an algorithm before coding it, we do a dry run: we follow the steps by hand with sample inputs.

text.en: Dry run: larger of a, b
IF a > b THEN big = a

say.en: Include tricky cases like equal values. Every row should give the expected output.
There are several ways to check if n is prime. Method 1 divides by every number from 2 to n minus 1.
Method 2 divides only up to n by 2. Method 3 stops at the square root of n, because a larger factor must pair with a smaller one.
For n equal to 97, method 1 needs 95 divisions but method 3 needs only 8. It has the smallest time complexity.

narration.en: We dry-run an algorithm with a trace table and compare how many divisions three prime-testing methods need.

body.en: There may be several correct algorithms for a problem. We compare them by time complexity (how much processing time, or how many steps, they need) and space complexity (how much memory they need). To check if n is prime, method 1 divides by 2 to n − 1, method 2 by 2 to n/2, and method 3 only by 2 to $\sqrt{n}$. Method 3 needs far fewer divisions, so it is the most efficient.

points.en: Time complexity: processing time / number of steps
Prime check up to √n is much faster than up to n − 1

title.en: How much work does each prime test do?

caption.en: Move n and compare the number of divisions each method needs in the worst case, when n is prime.

tryThis.en: Set n = 97 and check the board’s numbers.
Make n ten times larger: how much more work does method 3 do?
Why is it enough to test divisors up to √n?

narration.en: Move n and compare the number of divisions each method needs in the worst case, when n is prime. Set n = 97 and check the board’s numbers.

problem.en: How many divisions does each method need to confirm that 97 is prime?

steps.en: Method 1 divides by 2, 3, …, 96: that is 95 divisions.
Method 2 divides by 2 to 97 ÷ 2 = 48 (integer part): 47 divisions.
Method 3 divides by 2 to √97 ≈ 9.8, i.e. 2 to 9: only 8 divisions.

answer.en: 95, 47 and 8 divisions; method 3 is the most efficient.
